passage:
Saturday night. Pallavi cried on the terrace tonight about her dad's surgery, and every muscle in me wanted to say I had an assignment and leave. Instead I said it out loud: "I've got the urge to run right now. It's not you. I'm just bad at this." She laughed through her tears. I stayed twenty more minutes, which felt like two hours. Then, weirdly, I told her something I've never told anyone here: I hate my birthday because nobody at home ever remembered it. She didn't make a big deal. She just said, "Noted. I'll remember." Nothing bad happened. I'm writing this down so I believe it tomorrow.
Lakshmi

qa.q: How much longer did Lakshmi stay on the terrace?
qa.a: Twenty more minutes.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi feeling while Pallavi cried?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt a strong urge to flee and was uneasy with the closeness, but chose to name it and stay.

qa.q: Which step worked, and why?
qa.a: Saying the urge to run out loud, because it let Lakshmi stay without pretending and made a small honest disclosure possible.

qa.q: How might Pallavi feel hearing about the birthday?
qa.a: Pallavi probably feels trusted and touched, and her simple "I'll remember" shows she welcomes the need.

grounding: Shows an avoidant young adult naming the urge to withdraw, staying longer and making a small disclosure that is met kindly.

passage: At the Pushkar fair ground, Hansa bought two cups of chai and asked, "Aditi, why do you never talk about home?" Aditi felt the familiar pull: say "nothing to tell" and go and find the bus. She looked at the camel carts instead. Then she said, "I want to change the subject right now. I'm noticing that." Hansa waited, blowing on her tea. Aditi stayed, though her hands were cold. "My father left when I was eight. I've told nobody here." Hansa didn't gasp or grab her. She just nodded. "Thank you for telling me." They watched the lamps come on over the lake. Aditi's shoulders came down a little. On the bus back she messaged Hansa: "Same time next week?"

qa.q: Where did Hansa and Aditi drink chai?
qa.a: At the Pushkar fair ground.

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling when Hansa asked about home?
qa.a: She felt the familiar pull to escape and was nervous, with cold hands, yet chose to stay.

qa.q: What made it easier for Aditi to open up?

qa.q: How might Hansa see the message on the bus?

passage: For the first year I chased. Whenever my wife, Payal, went silent in a fight, I followed her from room to room: "What's wrong? Talk to me!" louder each time. She'd go to the balcony, then put her headphones on, then leave for a walk. I'm Rafiq, and I felt invisible in my own flat. One night a friend asked, "Does chasing ever work?" It never had. So I tried something else. When she went quiet about my mother's visit, I said once, calmly, "I need us to decide by Sunday. Can we talk after dinner?" Then I made tea. She came into the kitchen at nine. I also told her I won't keep having fights with a closed door. That limit is mine to keep.

qa.q: Where did Payal go first when Rafiq followed her?
qa.a: To the balcony.

qa.q: How did Rafiq feel during the year of chasing?
qa.a: Rafiq felt invisible and shut out, and grew louder as Payal withdrew further.

qa.q: What changed, and why did it work better?
qa.a: Rafiq made one calm, direct request with a time and then gave space, which let Payal come back on her own.

qa.q: What might it be like for Payal when Rafiq follows her from room to room?
qa.a: Payal likely feels cornered, so she retreats further to the balcony, headphones and walks.

grounding: Shows a partner who feels shut out, learns that chasing drives the other away, and uses a calm request and a personal limit.

passage: Session note, couple's session two. Vidya did most of the talking again. When she described last week's argument about Jagdish's late nights at the lab, he looked at the floor and said, "It's not a big deal." I watched her hands clench and her voice rise; she leaned forward, repeating herself. He leaned further back. I paused them and asked Vidya to say, slowly, one sentence about what she needed. She said, "When you go quiet, I feel alone. I need ten minutes of talk each night, even if it's short." Jagdish looked up for the first time. I noted her relief. Next step: both will try the ten minutes this week, and I will see Jagdish alone once to hear his side.

qa.q: What did Jagdish say about the argument?
qa.a: "It's not a big deal."

qa.q: What was Vidya feeling as she repeated herself?
qa.a: She felt alone and dismissed, with clenched hands and a rising voice.

qa.q: Why did the one slow sentence work better than repeating herself?
qa.a: A calm, specific request was easier for Jagdish to hear than pressure, so he looked up instead of leaning back.

qa.q: How might Jagdish experience Vidya leaning forward and repeating herself?
qa.a: He may feel pressured and retreat further, which is why he leaned back.

grounding: Illustrates a partner who feels shut out during conflict, and how a calm, direct request works better than chasing.

passage:
Thursday. Vandana did it again tonight. I said I felt hurt that she'd booked the trip without asking, and she said, "You're overthinking," and went to the balcony with her phone. Old me would have followed her out, pleaded, maybe cried, and she'd have gone even quieter. Tonight I didn't. I sat with my tea, heart thumping, and texted her from the sofa, ten feet away: "I'm not going to chase you. When you're ready, I want to talk about how we decide trips. I'll be up till eleven." At 10.20 she came in and sat at the other end of the sofa. We didn't solve it. But she stayed.
Sudha

passage: At the playgroup in Kraków, Pablo toddled towards his father at pickup, arms half up, then stopped dead a step away. He stared at the floor, frozen, then backed into the coat rack. Then in maths she said, "No, like this," and took my pencil, and something in me went BOOM. I threw the pencil box and shouted that she's stupid. Everybody looked. Then I couldn't talk at all, like my mouth was locked. Sir sent me outside. I hate being sent out, it makes the boom bigger. Pema came at lunch and gave me half her paratha anyway. I didn't say thank you because I didn't know how. I want her to be my friend. I'm scared she'll stop.

After the bell he sat on the step beside her, asked nothing, and said, "Tomorrow, tell me about the goat again." She shrugged. grounding: Illustrates a child switching from friendly to explosive to shut down, and how punishment deepens it while steady warmth helps.

passage: You know what I did to Abhinav? For three months he was my whole world. We talked every night; I told him things I'd never told anyone, about when my mother left. qa.a: Dolma may feel understood and less cornered, since the letter asks for nothing and leaves a door open.

grounding: Illustrates a friend who notices warm-then-cold shifts, reads them as fear, sets a boundary and suggests a trusted adult.

passage: So you know Santosh, from my tuition? Last month we were inseparable, I'm not exaggerating: walking home together, sharing notes, laughing about everything. Then one Tuesday he looked through me like I was a stranger. My first reaction was, fine, be like that. I'm Bidisha, and I don't beg. But I watched him that week. He was jumpy, snapping at everyone, not just me. I remembered him saying his older brother had moved abroad last year and he hated talking about it. So instead of getting angry, I told him, "I'm not going anywhere, but I won't be treated like dirt either." And then: "You should talk to Ma'am at tuition, or the school counsellor." He shrugged. The next day I saw him walk into the counsellor's room.

qa.q: What did Bidisha see Santosh do the next day?
qa.a: Walk into the counsellor's room.

qa.q: What was Bidisha feeling when Santosh first looked through her?
qa.a: She felt hurt and a bit proud and angry, thinking "fine, be like that", before seeing it differently.

qa.q: How did Bidisha balance kindness and limits?
qa.a: She stayed available, refused to be treated badly and encouraged him to talk to a trusted adult.

qa.q: Why might Santosh have gone cold after being close?
qa.a: He may be scared of losing people after his brother moved abroad, so closeness feels risky.

grounding: Shows a peer who sees a friend turn cold, reads it as fear, keeps a clear boundary and encourages a trusted adult.

passage: When Karthik texted, "I think I'm falling for you," Uma read it on the metro and felt two things at once: a rush of warmth, and the urge to throw the phone out of the window. By evening she had picked a fight over nothing and told him he was too needy; at midnight she sent a long message begging him not to go. Her flatmate Himani found her on the kitchen floor, crying. "I want this so much, and it feels like danger," Uma said. Himani didn't lecture. She made instant noodles, sat with her, and reminded her of the counsellor at the college wellness centre. "You liked her. Book it tomorrow. I'll walk you there." Uma nodded into her shoulder.

qa.q: Where did Uma read Karthik's text?
qa.a: On the metro.

qa.q: What two feelings did Uma have when she read the text?
qa.a: A rush of warmth and a sense of danger, wanting love yet scared of it coming close.

qa.q: How is Himani helping Uma build steadier support?
qa.a: By staying with her calmly and encouraging her to book the counsellor, offering to walk her there.

qa.q: How might Karthik feel after the fight and then the midnight message?
qa.a: Karthik is probably confused and hurt, being pushed away and then begged to stay on the same day.

grounding: Shows a young adult who longs for love but feels danger when it comes close, supported by a steady friend and a counsellor.

passage:
"You cancelled on her again?" Siddharth dropped onto Chinmay's hostel bed.
"She said she loves me, Sid. Out loud. In front of her friends."
"And that's bad?"
"No! It's all I've ever wanted." Chinmay pulled his knees up. "Then my chest went tight, like something terrible was coming. So I said I had a lab."
"You don't have labs on Sundays."
"I know." A long pause. "Last time I did this, I vanished for a week, then turned up at her door at midnight with flowers. She called it whiplash."
"We've played badminton every Wednesday for two years. I've never vanished on you, and you've never vanished on me."
"Because you're safe."
"So practise with safe people. And go back to that counsellor from first year."
"Will you come with me to book?"
"Wednesday. After badminton."

qa.q: What excuse did Chinmay give for cancelling?
qa.a: He said he had a lab.

qa.q: What did Chinmay feel when she said she loved him?
qa.a: He felt longing and joy, then a tight chest and dread, as if something terrible was coming.

qa.q: What steps does Siddharth suggest?
qa.a: Practising closeness with safe people and going back to the counsellor, with Siddharth coming along to book.

qa.q: What is it like for the girlfriend when Chinmay vanishes and then appears at midnight?
qa.a: She experiences it as whiplash, confused by the swing from distance to intensity.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult who wants love deeply but panics when it comes near, and turns to a steady friend and a counsellor.

passage: The day Tenzin said he'd move to Pune for me, I went cold all over. I'd dreamt of someone choosing me like that since I was small. My father came and went so often that I learned not to watch the door. So when it finally happened, I said, "Don't you dare," and didn't speak to him for four days. Then I missed him so badly I couldn't breathe, and called at two in the morning saying sorry, sorry. I'm Dolma, twenty-two. I've started seeing a therapist every other Thursday. And I have two friends from the hostel I've kept for five years, which is its own small miracle. I'm learning love doesn't always come with a door slamming.

qa.q: How often does Dolma see a therapist?
qa.a: Every other Thursday.

qa.q: What did Dolma feel when Tenzin offered to move?
qa.a: Dolma felt a cold fear alongside a long-held longing, because being chosen felt dangerous after a father who came and went.

qa.q: What is helping Dolma change the pattern?
qa.a: Regular sessions with a therapist and steady friendships kept for five years.

qa.q: How might Tenzin have felt during the four days of silence?
qa.a: Tenzin was probably hurt and confused, having offered a big commitment and met silence.

grounding: Shows a young adult longing for love yet feeling danger when it arrives, starting to change through a therapist and steady friends.

passage: Parul, you asked how I knew when to stop tiptoeing. When I was twenty-four I was engaged to Vinod. One week he'd send me poems and turn up at the bank with jasmine. The next he'd vanish, and when I called he'd say, "Why are you always after me?" I learned to watch his face before I spoke, to weigh every word. I stopped seeing my friends in case he needed me. My turning point was small: I fell ill with worry before an exam, and lying in that clinic I thought, I'm disappearing. I told him I loved him and that I'd keep my Sunday walks with my friends, no matter what. And I asked him, gently, to see a counsellor. We didn't marry, but I kept myself. That's Vandana-masi's one lesson.

qa.q: What did Vinod bring to the bank?
qa.a: Jasmine.

qa.q: What was young Vandana feeling while she watched Vinod's face before speaking?
qa.a: She felt anxious and confused, always on guard and afraid of setting off his coldness.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story?
qa.a: Falling ill before an exam made her see she was disappearing, so she kept her friends and asked Vinod to see a counsellor.

qa.q: How might Vinod have felt when Vandana kept her Sunday walks?
qa.a: Vinod may have felt unsettled or hurt, but also met a steady limit instead of her tiptoeing.

grounding: Shows a young adult confused by a partner's hot-and-cold behaviour, who protects her wellbeing and encourages professional help.

passage: With his accountancy exam six days away, Pranav couldn't afford another week like the last one. On Monday Asif had cooked his favourite biryani and kissed his forehead. By Wednesday he'd stopped speaking, slammed cupboards and slept on the sofa. Pranav caught himself tiptoeing to the fridge, rehearsing sentences before saying them, forgetting whole pages of notes. On Thursday he packed his books and told Asif, calmly, "I love you. I'm going to study at my sister's till the exam. I'm not leaving you; I'm looking after myself." Then, softer: "The ups and downs scare both of us. Will you talk to a counsellor about it?" Asif's jaw tightened. Then he nodded, once.

qa.q: Where did Pranav go to study?
qa.a: To his sister's.

qa.q: How was Pranav feeling during the week before he packed his books?
qa.a: He felt confused and on edge, tiptoeing and rehearsing sentences, so anxious he forgot pages of notes.

qa.q: Why was going to his sister's a wise step?
qa.a: It protected his wellbeing and exam while he stayed warm and consistent and encouraged professional help.

qa.q: What might Asif be feeling when he nods?
qa.a: Asif may feel hurt and scared, yet accept that the swings are hurting both of them.

grounding: Illustrates a partner confused by sudden affection then distance, who protects his wellbeing and encourages counselling.

passage: Irfan checked Naina's mood the way other people checked the weather. On Friday she'd hugged him at the door of their Hyderabad flat and planned a trip to Coorg; on Sunday she wouldn't look at him and called him clingy for asking why. At lunch on Monday, his friend Sahil noticed him rewording a message for the tenth time. "You're walking on eggshells, bhai." Irfan admitted he'd stopped going to cricket in case she needed him. Sahil said, "You can't fix her by shrinking. Keep your cricket. Be steady. And ask her, kindly, to talk to someone who can help." That evening Irfan went to cricket, came home at nine as promised, and told Naina he loved her and hoped she'd see a counsellor.

qa.q: What had Irfan stopped doing?
qa.a: Going to cricket.

qa.q: What was Irfan feeling as he reworded the message for the tenth time?
qa.a: He was anxious and confused, afraid of setting off Naina's coldness.

qa.q: What did Sahil advise, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Keep cricket, be steady and kindly suggest help, because Irfan cannot fix Naina by shrinking himself.

qa.q: How might Naina feel when Irfan comes home at nine as promised?
qa.a: Naina may feel reassured by his consistency, even if the suggestion of a counsellor is hard to hear.

grounding: Shows a partner walking on eggshells in a hot-and-cold bond who protects his own life, stays consistent and encourages professional help.
